title: 🧊 States of Matter Lab
description: Welcome to the States of Matter Lab! You are a Grade 6 student stepping into the chemistry lab for a 14-week adventure. Starting with the basics of solids, liquids, and gases, you will explore how matter changes state when heated or cooled. Observe particles dancing, watch ice melt, see water boil, and discover condensation on cold surfaces. Handle lab crises, master the particle model, and showcase your knowledge at the school Science Day. Can you become the Matter Master?
subject: chemistry
how_to_play: You are a Grade 6 student exploring states of matter over a 14-week chemistry lab program.
Each week presents a lab challenge with choices that affect your knowledge, safety, and creativity.
Watch your dashboard — your Lab Stations (Heating, Cooling, Observation, Measurement, Particle Modelling) are interconnected.
NPCs like Dr. Kelvin (teacher), Frosty (lab mascot), Priya, and Arjun react to your decisions.
Random events like equipment malfunctions and guest scientists will test your adaptability.
Keep your Safety Compliance high — if it drops too low, you will lose lab privileges!
learning_objectives: Identify and describe the three states of matter: solid, liquid, and gas
Explain how particles are arranged and move in each state of matter
Understand the processes of melting, freezing, boiling, evaporation, and condensation
Relate temperature changes to changes in state of matter
Practice safe laboratory procedures when using heat sources
Apply the particle model to explain everyday phenomena
cultural_context: School chemistry laboratory, hands-on STEM learning, collaborative experimentation with everyday materials

simulation_config.ai_scene_prompt_template: A Grade 6 school chemistry lab, knowledge level {knowledge_level}%, safety awareness {safety_awareness}%, lab supplies at {lab_supplies}%, observation skill {observation_skill}%. Lab benches with beakers, thermometers, Bunsen burners, and ice.

rounds.round_title: Week 1: Welcome to the Matter Lab
rounds.situation: It is your first day in the chemistry lab! The benches are covered with beakers, thermometers, ice cubes, and mysterious containers. Dr. Kelvin welcomes the class and holds up three objects — a rock, a glass of water, and a balloon. 'Everything around you is made of matter,' he says. 'And matter comes in three main states. Before we explore them, we need to learn how to stay safe.' How do you want to start?
rounds.goal: Choose how to begin your exploration of states of matter.
rounds.coaching_moment: Delayed gratification: Spending time on fundamentals now will make every future experiment easier and safer.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why is it important to understand safety rules before handling Bunsen burners and hot liquids?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students entering a bright chemistry lab for the first time, lab benches with beakers and thermometers, teacher holding a rock glass of water and balloon

choices.label: A. Matter exists in three common states: solid, liquid, and gas

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Correctly identifying all three states shows you can see the full picture before diving into details.

choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Matter exists in three common states: solid, liquid, and gas. Everything around you — from your desk (solid) to the water you drink (liquid) to the air you breathe (gas) — is made of tiny particles called atoms and molecules arranged differently in each state.

choices.label: B. Matter only exists as solids and liquids because gases are invisible

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Dismissing gases as non-matter misses a key category, weakening your overall classification framework.

choices.feedback: 💡 Not quite! Even though gases are invisible, they are still matter. Gases have mass and take up space. You can feel wind (moving gas) and blow up a balloon with air. Matter exists in three common states: solid, liquid, and gas.

choices.label: C. Matter is only found in things you can see and touch

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Relying only on what you can see limits your ability to classify matter systematically.

choices.feedback: 💡 Not quite! Matter includes things you cannot easily see, like air and steam. If something has mass and takes up space, it is matter. Air is invisible but you can feel it when the wind blows — that proves it is real matter in the gas state.

choices.label: D. Liquids and gases are the same state because both can flow

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Grouping liquids and gases together overlooks a key difference, showing incomplete analysis of the evidence.

choices.feedback: 💡 Good thinking that both can flow, but they are different states! Liquids have a definite volume (a cup of water stays a cup), while gases expand to fill any container. Pour water into a box — it stays at the bottom. Gas would spread everywhere inside.

rounds.situation: Dr. Kelvin has set up a Solids Investigation Station with a wooden block, metal spoon, rubber ball, salt crystal, chalk, and chocolate. 'All solids, but with very different properties,' he says. 'Investigate what makes a solid a solid.' How do you begin?
rounds.goal: Investigate the properties of solids and understand particle arrangement.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Systematic investigation builds a stronger foundation.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What makes a solid different from a liquid at the particle level?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students examining various solid objects with magnifying glasses at a chemistry lab bench

choices.label: A. Particles in a solid are tightly packed and vibrate in fixed positions

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Linking particle arrangement to observable solid properties shows systematic cause-and-effect reasoning.

choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ In solids, particles are packed closely together in a regular pattern. They do not move freely — they only vibrate in their fixed positions. This is why solids have a definite shape and a definite volume. Think of them like students sitting in their seats, wiggling but not getting up!

choices.label: B. Particles in a solid are completely still and do not move at all

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Assuming particles are completely still overlooks subtle vibration, missing a critical detail in the model.

choices.feedback: 💡 Close, but particles in a solid are never completely still! They constantly vibrate in their fixed positions. Even in ice, the water molecules are jiggling slightly. If they stopped moving entirely, the temperature would be absolute zero (−273°C), which has never been reached.

choices.label: C. Particles in a solid are loosely packed and can slide past each other

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Confusing solid and liquid particle behaviour shows a gap in distinguishing between the two models.

choices.feedback: 💡 That actually describes a liquid, not a solid! In liquids, particles are close together but can slide past one another. In solids, particles are tightly packed in fixed positions and can only vibrate. That is why a book keeps its shape but water takes the shape of its container.

choices.label: D. Solids have a definite shape because they are heavy, not because of particles

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Blaming weight instead of particle forces means you are looking at the wrong cause for the effect.

choices.feedback: 💡 Weight does not determine shape! A feather is very light but keeps its shape because it is a solid. Solids have a definite shape because their particles are locked in fixed positions by strong forces of attraction. A heavy liquid like mercury still takes the shape of its container.

rounds.situation: Today the lab is about liquids! Dr. Kelvin has prepared water, cooking oil, honey, milk, and liquid soap. 'They all flow, but differently,' he says. Priya notices the honey is barely moving while water splashes easily. How do you explore liquids?
rounds.goal: Explore the properties of liquids and understand how they differ from solids and gases.
rounds.coaching_moment: Observation skill: Careful observation is the first step to understanding science.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do liquids take the shape of their container but solids do not?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students pouring different liquids of varying viscosities into containers in a chemistry lab

choices.label: A. Liquids have a definite volume but take the shape of their container

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Recognising that liquids keep volume but change shape shows precise comparison across states.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Understanding how liquids adjust to their container mirrors flexible thinking in new situations.

choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Liquids have a definite volume — 200 mL of water stays 200 mL whether it is in a glass, a bowl, or a bottle. But liquids take the shape of whatever container they are in because their particles can slide past each other freely. This makes liquids great at flowing!

choices.label: B. Liquids have no definite volume and expand to fill any container

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Mixing up gas and liquid properties reveals a need to compare states more carefully before deciding.

choices.feedback: 💡 That describes a gas, not a liquid! Gases expand to fill their entire container. Liquids have a definite volume — pour 500 mL of juice into a 1-litre bottle and it only fills half. The liquid particles are close together, so they cannot spread out like gas particles do.

choices.label: C. Liquids have both a definite shape and a definite volume

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Assigning solid traits to liquids shows the importance of checking each property against the evidence.

choices.feedback: 💡 That describes a solid! Liquids have a definite volume (200 mL stays 200 mL), but they do NOT have a definite shape. Pour water from a round cup into a square box — the water changes shape. Liquid particles can slide past each other, so the liquid flows to match its container.

choices.label: D. Liquids cannot flow because their particles are packed tightly

skill_explanation.adaptability: Discovering that packed particles can still flow challenges a rigid assumption and requires updating your mental model.

choices.feedback: 💡 Actually, liquids can flow very well! Their particles are close together, but they can slide past one another. This is why you can pour water, milk, and juice. Viscosity measures how easily a liquid flows — honey flows slowly (high viscosity) while water flows quickly (low viscosity).

rounds.situation: Dr. Kelvin sets up the Gas Discovery Lab with balloons, syringes, and sealed containers. He pushes a beaker upside-down into water — the water does not fill it. 'Air — a gas — is taking up space in there!' Arjun is amazed. How do you investigate gases?
rounds.goal: Discover the properties of gases and understand how gas particles behave.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: Proving something invisible exists requires creative experimental design.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How can you prove that air has mass and takes up space?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students doing balloon and syringe experiments with gases, teacher demonstrating with a beaker and water tank

choices.label: A. Gas particles are spread far apart and move rapidly in all directions
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ In gases, particles are very far apart compared to solids and liquids. They move rapidly in random directions, bouncing off each other and the walls of their container. This is why gases have no definite shape or volume — they spread out to fill whatever space is available, like perfume spreading across a room!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: B. Gas particles are packed together tightly but move in circles
choices.feedback: 💡 Not quite! Gas particles are actually very far apart, not tightly packed. There are large spaces between them, which is why gases can be easily compressed (squeezed). They move in straight lines in random directions (not circles), bouncing off each other like billiard balls.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. Gases do not have mass because you cannot feel or see them
choices.feedback: 💡 Gases definitely have mass! You can prove this: weigh a deflated balloon, then inflate it and weigh again — it is heavier. Air (a gas) pushes down on us with atmospheric pressure. You feel wind because moving air has mass and energy. All matter, including gases, has mass.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. Gases keep a fixed shape just like solids but are lighter
choices.feedback: 💡 Gases have no definite shape at all! They spread to fill their entire container. Open a perfume bottle in one corner of a room and eventually you can smell it everywhere — the gas particles spread in all directions. Being lighter does not mean keeping a shape; shape depends on how particles are arranged.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: The Heating Station is buzzing! Each team has ice cubes, chocolate, butter, wax, and thermometers. 'Melt things and record exactly when they change state,' says Dr. Kelvin. 'Track the temperature every 30 seconds.' What is your approach?
rounds.goal: Understand melting and freezing as changes of state and measure melting points.
rounds.coaching_moment: Delayed gratification: Recording careful data now leads to much better understanding later.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What happens to the particles in a solid when it reaches its melting point?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students heating ice and chocolate with thermometers, recording temperatures on graphs

challenge.question: Water freezes at 0°C and boils at 100°C. If you start with water at 25°C, how many degrees must it cool down to reach its freezing point?
challenge.formula_hint: Temperature change = starting temperature − target temperature

choices.label: A. Melting is when a solid gains heat energy and changes to a liquid
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ When a solid is heated, its particles gain energy and vibrate faster. At the melting point, particles get enough energy to break free from their fixed positions and begin sliding past each other, forming a liquid. Ice melts at 0°C. Freezing is the reverse — a liquid loses heat and becomes a solid.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: B. Melting happens when liquid particles slow down and lock into place
choices.feedback: 💡 You have described freezing, not melting! When particles slow down and lock into fixed positions, a liquid becomes a solid. Melting is the opposite: a solid gains heat energy, particles vibrate faster, and they break free to become a liquid. Remember: melting = solid → liquid.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. Ice melts at 100°C, which is why it takes a long time to melt
choices.feedback: 💡 Ice melts at 0°C, not 100°C! 100°C is the boiling point of water (when liquid water becomes steam). The melting point and freezing point of water are both 0°C — it is the same temperature. Ice starts to melt as soon as the temperature rises above 0°C.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Water expands when it freezes because the particles move faster
choices.feedback: 💡 Water does expand when it freezes, but not because particles move faster! Actually, they slow down. Water is special: when it freezes, its molecules arrange into a crystal structure that takes up MORE space than liquid water. This is why ice floats and why pipes can burst in winter.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

rounds.situation: Dr. Kelvin explains: 'There are TWO ways a liquid can become a gas — boiling and evaporation. But they are very different!' He places wet paper towels near a fan, on a table, and in the sun. How do you investigate?
rounds.goal: Compare evaporation and boiling and understand the factors that affect evaporation.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Understanding the difference between similar concepts is a key scientific skill.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do wet clothes dry on a clothesline even though they never reach 100 degrees Celsius?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students observing boiling water with bubbles and steam, and wet cloths drying at room temperature

choices.label: A. Evaporation happens only at the surface of a liquid and can occur below boiling point
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Evaporation happens only at the liquid surface when fast-moving particles escape into the air. It can happen at any temperature! Boiling, on the other hand, happens throughout the entire liquid at a specific temperature (100°C for water). Wet clothes dry on a clothesline because of evaporation, not boiling.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: B. Evaporation and boiling are the same thing — both mean a liquid turns to gas
choices.feedback: 💡 Both involve liquid becoming gas, but they are different! Evaporation happens only at the surface, at any temperature, and is slow. Boiling happens throughout the whole liquid at a specific temperature and produces bubbles. A puddle drying up is evaporation; a kettle making bubbles is boiling.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. Water can only become a gas when it reaches exactly 100°C
choices.feedback: 💡 Water becomes a gas through evaporation at temperatures well below 100°C! That is how puddles dry up on a warm day and how your wet hair dries. The fastest-moving particles at the surface escape into the air. 100°C is just the boiling point, where the whole liquid turns to gas rapidly.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. Boiling happens at the surface of a liquid while evaporation happens inside
choices.feedback: 💡 You have it backwards! Evaporation happens at the surface of the liquid. Boiling happens throughout the entire liquid — that is why you see bubbles forming inside the water and rising up. Remember: evaporation = surface only, boiling = everywhere inside.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: Emergency! A water pipe has burst near the Heating Station. The lab is flooded and some experiments are ruined. Dr. Kelvin says calmly: 'The evaporating water is cooling the room — can you explain why?' How do you respond?
rounds.goal: Apply knowledge of temperature and particle motion to a real-world situation.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: Real scientists use setbacks as learning opportunities.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How does evaporating water cool down the surroundings?
rounds.image_prompt: A flooded chemistry lab with students and teacher calmly addressing the situation

choices.label: A. When temperature increases, particles move faster and gain more kinetic energy
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Temperature is actually a measure of how fast particles are moving. When you heat something, you are giving its particles more kinetic energy, making them move faster. This is why matter expands when heated — faster-moving particles push each other further apart. Understanding this helps you stay safe in the lab!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.resilience: Pushing through difficulty builds mental strength.

choices.label: B. Temperature has no effect on how particles move inside matter
choices.feedback: 💡 Temperature is directly connected to particle movement! Higher temperature means particles move faster, lower temperature means they move slower. This is the whole reason matter changes state — heat ice enough and the particles vibrate so fast they break free and flow as liquid water.

skill_explanation.resilience: Choosing to persist when things get hard develops resilience.

choices.label: C. Heating a substance makes its particles grow bigger in size
choices.feedback: 💡 The particles themselves do not grow bigger! When heated, particles move faster and the spaces between them increase. This is called thermal expansion. A metal railway track expands in summer not because its iron atoms get bigger, but because they vibrate more and push further apart.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: D. Cold objects have no particle movement at all
choices.feedback: 💡 Even very cold objects have particles that are still moving! Particles only stop moving at absolute zero (−273.15°C), which has never actually been reached. Ice at 0°C has particles vibrating in place. Cold just means slower movement, not zero movement.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: Dr. Kelvin brings cold lemonade to class. Water droplets appear on the outside of the glass. 'Where did this water come from?' he asks. Priya says, 'It is the opposite of evaporation!' How do you investigate condensation?
rounds.goal: Understand condensation as the reverse of evaporation and identify it in daily life.
rounds.coaching_moment: Observation skill: The best scientists notice what others overlook.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do water droplets form on the outside of a cold glass on a warm day?
rounds.image_prompt: Cold glass of lemonade with condensation droplets on a lab bench, students observing closely

challenge.question: You heat 500 g of water from 20°C to 100°C. How many degrees did the temperature rise?
challenge.formula_hint: Temperature rise = final temperature − initial temperature

choices.label: A. Water droplets forming on a cold glass of lemonade is condensation — gas turning to liquid
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Condensation is when a gas cools down and changes to a liquid. The water vapor in warm air touches the cold glass surface, loses energy, and the water molecules slow down enough to form liquid droplets. This is the same process that forms morning dew on grass and clouds in the sky!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

choices.label: B. The water on a cold glass leaks through the glass from the lemonade inside
choices.feedback: 💡 The glass is solid and waterproof — liquid cannot leak through it! The water droplets come from the air around the glass. Water vapor (gas) in the warm air touches the cold surface, loses heat energy, and condenses into tiny liquid droplets. Try it: a dry glass gets wet on the outside when cold!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. Condensation is when a liquid heats up and becomes a gas
choices.feedback: 💡 You have described evaporation, which is the opposite of condensation! Condensation is gas → liquid (cooling down). Evaporation is liquid → gas (heating up). A good way to remember: CONdensation = gas CONtracts into liquid. Think of steam hitting a cold mirror and forming water drops.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. Condensation only happens when water reaches 0°C and freezes
choices.feedback: 💡 Condensation and freezing are different processes! Condensation is gas → liquid and can happen at many temperatures. Water vapor condenses into dew at 15°C on cool mornings. Freezing is liquid → solid and happens at 0°C for water. Both involve cooling, but they produce different states.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Being open to new information and changing course builds adaptability.

rounds.situation: Model Building Day! Dr. Kelvin challenges every team to create a model showing how particles are arranged in solids, liquids, and gases. Materials include clay balls, marbles, springs, and craft supplies. How do you build your model?
rounds.goal: Build and explain a particle model showing the arrangement of particles in all three states.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: Building models helps you visualize and communicate scientific ideas.
rounds.reflection_prompt: How does the particle model explain why gases can be compressed but solids cannot?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students building particle models with clay balls and marbles

choices.label: A. The particle model explains that all matter is made of tiny particles with spaces between them
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ The particle model states that all matter is made of incredibly tiny particles (atoms and molecules) with spaces between them. In solids, particles are close with small spaces. In liquids, spaces are a bit larger. In gases, spaces are very large. This model helps explain why gases can be compressed but solids cannot!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.
skill_explanation.creativity: Exploring an unconventional approach shows creative thinking.

choices.label: B. Matter is a continuous solid substance with no gaps or spaces inside
choices.feedback: 💡 This was actually what people believed centuries ago! But scientists proved that all matter is made of tiny particles with spaces between them. Evidence: you can dissolve sugar in water (sugar particles fit between water particles), and you can compress a gas (particles move closer together).

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: C. Particles in a gas are smaller than particles in a solid of the same substance
choices.feedback: 💡 The particles themselves are the same size in all three states! A water molecule is the same size whether it is in ice, liquid water, or steam. What changes is the spacing between particles and how fast they move. Gas particles are far apart, not smaller.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: D. The particle model only applies to gases, not to solids or liquids
choices.feedback: 💡 The particle model applies to ALL states of matter! Solids, liquids, and gases are all made of particles. The difference is how those particles are arranged and how they move. In solids, particles vibrate in place; in liquids, they slide; in gases, they zoom around freely.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

rounds.situation: Dr. Kelvin shows dry ice (solid CO2) turning directly to gas. 'This is sublimation!' He also shows frost forming on a cold plate. 'And this is deposition — gas to solid directly!' How do you approach this challenge?
rounds.goal: Explore sublimation, deposition, and the complete range of state changes.
rounds.coaching_moment: Adaptability: Science is full of exceptions to simple rules — be ready to update your understanding.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Can you name a state change that skips a step? Why does it happen?
rounds.image_prompt: Dry ice smoking on a lab bench, frost crystals forming on a cold plate, students watching

choices.label: A. Sublimation is when a solid changes directly to a gas without becoming a liquid first
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Sublimation is when a solid skips the liquid stage and goes directly to gas. Dry ice (solid CO2) is a great example — it turns directly into carbon dioxide gas, which is why it creates that cool fog effect. Mothballs also sublime: they slowly shrink as the solid turns to gas without ever melting.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Pivoting your strategy when needed is a sign of adaptive thinking.

choices.label: B. Sublimation is when a gas changes directly to a solid
choices.feedback: 💡 You have described deposition, which is the reverse of sublimation! Sublimation is solid → gas directly. Deposition is gas → solid directly. Frost forming on a window in winter is deposition — water vapor turns directly into ice crystals without first becoming liquid water.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. Matter can only change state in this order: solid → liquid → gas
choices.feedback: 💡 Matter can change state in many directions! Solid → liquid (melting), liquid → gas (evaporation), and also backwards: gas → liquid (condensation), liquid → solid (freezing). Plus, sublimation skips a step: solid → gas directly. State changes can go in any direction depending on energy.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Responding to unexpected situations with creativity shows adaptability.

choices.label: D. During any state change, the substance becomes a completely different material
choices.feedback: 💡 Changing state is a physical change, not a chemical one! Ice, water, and steam are all still H2O — the same substance. Only the arrangement and movement of particles changes. You can always reverse a state change (melt ice back to water, freeze water back to ice).

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

rounds.situation: Dr. Kelvin heats a metal ball that no longer fits through a ring it passed through when cold. 'Temperature can make matter expand, contract, and change density!' he says. How do you investigate?
rounds.goal: Understand thermal expansion, contraction, and how temperature affects density.
rounds.coaching_moment: Strategic thinking: Understanding thermal expansion helps engineers design safer bridges.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why are there gaps between railway track sections?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students observing thermal expansion experiments, heated metal ball, expanding liquid in a tube

challenge.question: A substance has a mass of 200 g and occupies 250 cm³. What is its density in g/cm³?

choices.label: A. Most substances expand when heated because their particles move apart, making them less dense
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ When heated, particles gain energy and move faster, pushing further apart. This increases the volume (expansion) while the mass stays the same, so the density decreases. This is why hot air rises (less dense) and why there are gaps in railway tracks and bridges — to allow for expansion in summer!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.
skill_explanation.adaptability: Flexibility in your thinking helps you handle change effectively.

choices.label: B. Heating a substance adds more particles, which makes it expand
choices.feedback: 💡 Heating does NOT add particles! The number of particles stays exactly the same. What changes is the spacing between them. Heated particles move faster and push further apart, increasing volume. The same number of particles now takes up more space, which is why heated objects appear to grow.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. Water is denser as ice than as liquid, which is why ice sinks
choices.feedback: 💡 This is backwards! Ice floats because it is LESS dense than liquid water. Water is a special exception — most substances are denser as solids, but water molecules form an open crystal structure when frozen that takes up more space. This is why ice cubes float in your drink and icebergs float in the ocean!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. Metals contract when heated, which is why bridges need expansion joints
choices.feedback: 💡 Metals expand when heated, not contract! Bridges have expansion joints to give the metal room to grow in hot weather. Without these gaps, the bridge could buckle and crack. Metal railway tracks also have small gaps between sections. Metals contract (shrink) when they cool down.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

rounds.situation: The lab freezer has broken down! Ice samples melted and frozen water bottles burst. Dr. Kelvin asks: 'Why would a sealed bottle break when water freezes?' Arjun remembers water is special. How do you handle this?
rounds.goal: Apply knowledge of water's unique properties and the fourth state of matter.
rounds.coaching_moment: Resilience: When things go wrong, look for the science lesson hidden inside the problem.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Why do water pipes sometimes burst in winter?
rounds.image_prompt: Broken frozen water bottles in a lab, students examining burst containers, teacher explaining

choices.label: A. Water is unusual because it expands when it freezes, unlike most other substances
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Water is one of the very few substances that expand when freezing. Most substances contract (shrink) when they solidify. Water molecules form a hexagonal crystal structure in ice that has more space between molecules than liquid water. This is why frozen pipes burst and why ice floats — protecting aquatic life in winter!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.
skill_explanation.resilience: Learning from setbacks rather than giving up shows resilience.

choices.label: B. All substances expand when they freeze, just like water does
choices.feedback: 💡 Most substances actually contract (shrink) when they freeze! Water is special and unusual. When most liquids become solids, their particles pack more tightly, taking up less space. Water does the opposite because of its unique molecular structure. This special property of water is vital for life on Earth.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.

choices.label: C. Plasma is just another name for a very hot gas
choices.feedback: 💡 Plasma is actually a distinct fourth state of matter, not just hot gas! When gas is heated to extremely high temperatures, its atoms lose electrons and become electrically charged (ionized). This creates plasma, which behaves differently from regular gas. Lightning, the Sun, and neon signs all contain plasma.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: D. Ice sinks in water because solids are always heavier than liquids
choices.feedback: 💡 Ice actually floats in water! Whether something sinks or floats depends on density, not weight. Ice is less dense than liquid water because of its open crystal structure. A steel ship floats despite being heavy because its overall density (including air inside) is less than water. Density = mass / volume.

skill_explanation.resilience: Staying focused under pressure builds your ability to bounce back.

rounds.situation: One week before Science Day! Each team prepares a presentation connecting states of matter to everyday life: cooking, weather, thermometers, the water cycle. What is your presentation about?
rounds.goal: Apply states of matter concepts to real-world examples and prepare for Science Day.
rounds.coaching_moment: Creativity: The best scientists can explain complex ideas in simple, everyday terms.
rounds.reflection_prompt: Can you name five everyday examples of matter changing state?
rounds.image_prompt: Grade 6 students preparing science presentations with posters, models of clouds and thermometers

choices.label: A. Cooking an egg involves heat energy changing the liquid egg white into a solid
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ When you cook an egg, the heat energy changes the proteins in the liquid egg white, causing them to unfold and bond together, forming a solid. While this is actually a chemical change (the proteins change permanently), it beautifully shows how heat energy transforms the state of everyday materials. You cannot uncook an egg!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.
skill_explanation.creativity: Looking at the problem from a new angle demonstrates creativity.

choices.label: B. A thermometer works because the liquid inside it freezes when the temperature changes
choices.feedback: 💡 Thermometers do not work by freezing! They use thermal expansion. The liquid inside (usually mercury or alcohol) expands when heated and contracts when cooled. As the liquid expands, it rises up the narrow tube. The height of the liquid tells you the temperature. Freezing the liquid would break the thermometer!

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

choices.label: C. Clouds are made of water vapor, which is an invisible gas
choices.feedback: 💡 Clouds are NOT water vapor! Water vapor is invisible. Clouds are made of tiny liquid water droplets (or ice crystals) that formed when water vapor condensed in the cold upper atmosphere. You can see clouds because they are made of liquid droplets, not gas. The invisible water vapor condensed into visible droplets.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Considering long-term impact before acting builds strategic thinking.

choices.label: D. Morning dew on grass is an example of evaporation happening overnight
choices.feedback: 💡 Dew is actually an example of condensation, not evaporation! At night, the ground cools down. When the air near the grass cools below a certain temperature (the dew point), water vapor in the air condenses into tiny liquid droplets on the cold grass surfaces. Condensation = gas → liquid.

skill_explanation.adaptability: Adjusting your approach when conditions change shows flexibility.

rounds.situation: Science Day! Parents, teachers, and younger students visit the lab. Dr. Kelvin announces: 'These students have gone from not knowing what matter is to understanding particles, state changes, and even plasma!' How do you present your knowledge?
rounds.goal: Showcase your complete understanding of states of matter at the Science Day event.
rounds.coaching_moment: Empathy: Great communicators adapt their explanations to their audience.
rounds.reflection_prompt: What was the most surprising thing you learned about states of matter?
rounds.image_prompt: School Science Day event with students presenting to parents about states of matter, celebratory atmosphere

choices.label: A. Plasma is the fourth state of matter, found in lightning, the Sun, and neon signs
choices.learning_concept: Plasma — the fourth state of matter
choices.feedback: Correct! ✅ Plasma is the fourth state of matter, formed when gas is heated to extremely high temperatures and its atoms become electrically charged (ionized). Plasma is actually the most common state of matter in the universe — stars are made of plasma! On Earth, you see plasma in lightning bolts, neon signs, and plasma TVs.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Weighing multiple outcomes before deciding strengthens your planning skills.
skill_explanation.creativity: Combining ideas in unexpected ways shows innovative thinking.

choices.label: B. There are only three states of matter: solid, liquid, and gas
choices.feedback: 💡 There is actually a fourth state: plasma! When gas is heated to very high temperatures, the atoms become ionized (they lose electrons). This creates plasma, which behaves differently from regular gas. Most of the visible matter in the universe is plasma — every star, including our Sun, is a giant ball of plasma.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Looking beyond the obvious choice shows you think strategically.

choices.label: C. The boiling point of a substance changes depending on how much of it you have
choices.learning_concept: Boiling point as a fixed property
choices.feedback: 💡 The boiling point of a pure substance is fixed and does not change with the amount. One cup of water and a whole bathtub of water both boil at 100°C at sea level. However, boiling point can change with altitude (lower on mountains) or if you add substances like salt. More water just takes longer to boil.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Planning your approach carefully is a sign of strategic reasoning.

choices.label: D. When water boils, the bubbles rising are filled with air, not water vapor
choices.feedback: 💡 The large bubbles you see when water boils are actually filled with water vapor (gaseous water), not air! As the liquid water reaches 100°C, water molecules throughout the liquid gain enough energy to become gas, forming bubbles of water vapor that rise to the surface and escape into the air.

skill_explanation.strategic_thinking: Thinking ahead about consequences shows strategic planning ability.

phases.description: Learn the basics: three states of matter, solids, liquids, gases, and melting

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 1: Basics of Matter
checkpoints.description: Let us see how well you understand solids, liquids, gases, and melting before moving on!
checkpoints.review_summary: You covered the three states of matter (solid, liquid, gas), how particles are arranged in each state, properties of liquids and gases, and the process of melting and freezing. Solids have tightly packed particles that vibrate in place. Liquids have particles that slide past each other, giving them a definite volume but no fixed shape. Gas particles are spread far apart and move rapidly in all directions. Melting happens when a solid gains enough heat energy for particles to break free and flow as a liquid.

questions.question: What are the three common states of matter?

choices.text: Solid, liquid, and gas
Hard, soft, and invisible
Hot, warm, and cold

questions.explanation: Matter exists in three common states: solid (definite shape and volume), liquid (definite volume, no fixed shape), and gas (no definite shape or volume). There is also a fourth state called plasma, but the three common ones are solid, liquid, and gas.

questions.question: How do particles behave in a solid?

choices.text: They float around freely in all directions
They are tightly packed and vibrate in fixed positions
They are completely still and do not move at all

questions.explanation: In a solid, particles are packed closely together in a regular pattern and vibrate in fixed positions. They never stop moving completely — that would only happen at absolute zero, which has never been reached. This tight arrangement is why solids have a definite shape.

questions.question: Why do liquids take the shape of their container?

choices.text: Because liquid particles can slide past each other
Because liquids have no mass
Because liquids expand to fill all the space like gases

questions.explanation: Liquid particles are close together but can slide past one another, allowing the liquid to flow and take the shape of its container. Unlike gases, liquids do NOT expand to fill all the available space — they have a definite volume. Pour 200 mL of water into a 1-litre bottle and it only fills part of it.

questions.question: At what temperature does ice melt into water?

choices.text: 100 degrees Celsius
50 degrees Celsius
0 degrees Celsius

questions.explanation: Ice melts at 0 degrees Celsius. This is the melting point of water. At this temperature, the particles in ice gain enough energy to break free from their fixed positions and start sliding past each other as liquid water. 100 degrees Celsius is the boiling point, not the melting point.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 2: State Changes and the Particle Model
checkpoints.description: Time to check your understanding of evaporation, condensation, sublimation, and the particle model!
checkpoints.review_summary: You explored evaporation (liquid to gas at the surface, at any temperature), boiling (liquid to gas throughout the liquid at a specific temperature), condensation (gas to liquid when cooled), temperature and particle motion (higher temperature means faster-moving particles), the particle model (all matter is made of tiny particles with spaces between them), and sublimation (solid to gas directly, skipping the liquid stage). You also learned that state changes are physical changes — the substance stays the same, only the particle arrangement changes.

questions.question: What is the difference between evaporation and boiling?

choices.text: They are the same process with different names
Evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid at a specific temperature
Evaporation only happens at 100 degrees Celsius

questions.explanation: Evaporation is a slow process that happens only at the surface of a liquid and can occur at any temperature — this is how puddles dry up and wet clothes dry on a line. Boiling is rapid and happens throughout the entire liquid at a specific temperature (100 degrees Celsius for water at sea level), producing bubbles.

questions.question: Water droplets forming on the outside of a cold glass is an example of which process?

choices.text: Evaporation
Condensation
Sublimation

questions.explanation: This is condensation — water vapor (gas) in the warm air touches the cold glass surface, loses energy, and changes from gas to liquid, forming droplets. Condensation is the reverse of evaporation. The same process forms morning dew on grass and clouds in the sky.

questions.question: What happens to particles when the temperature of a substance increases?

choices.text: The particles grow bigger in size
The particles stop moving
The particles move faster and gain more kinetic energy

questions.explanation: When temperature increases, particles gain kinetic energy and move faster. The particles themselves do not change size — the spaces between them increase as they move more energetically. This is why substances expand when heated (thermal expansion). Temperature is really a measure of average particle speed.

questions.question: What is sublimation?

choices.text: A solid changing directly to a gas without becoming a liquid first
A gas changing directly to a solid
A liquid changing to a solid when cooled

questions.explanation: Sublimation is when a solid changes directly into a gas, skipping the liquid stage entirely. Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) is a classic example — it turns directly into CO2 gas, creating that cool fog effect. Mothballs also sublime over time. The reverse process (gas directly to solid) is called deposition.

glossary_terms.definition: Anything that has mass and takes up space.
A state of matter with a definite shape and volume. Particles are tightly packed and vibrate in fixed positions.
A state of matter with a definite volume but no fixed shape. Particles can slide past each other.
A state of matter with no definite shape or volume. Particles move freely and fill their container.
The fourth state of matter, formed when gas is heated to extreme temperatures and atoms become ionized.
The change of state from solid to liquid when heat energy is added.
The change of state from liquid to solid when heat energy is removed.
The rapid change from liquid to gas throughout the liquid at the boiling point.
The slow change from liquid to gas at the surface, at any temperature.
The change of state from gas to liquid when a gas cools down.
The change from solid directly to gas without becoming a liquid.
A model explaining matter as tiny particles with spaces between them.
